documents: Published paper: Van Wyk de Vries et al. (2022), Physical Limnology and Sediment Dynamics of Lago Argentino, the World's Largest Ice-Contact Lake, JGR Earth Surface 127, e2022JF006598 (PDF, 22 pages; supplement not supplied)

entry.evidence: Carrivick and Tweed (2013) highlighted the lack of detailed limnological and sedimentological assessments of proglacial lakes.

steps.action: Frame the gap in limnological and sedimentological knowledge of large ice-contact lakes and take Lago Argentino as the case study.
steps.quote: Carrivick and Tweed (2013) highlighted the lack of detailed limnological and sedimentological assessments of proglacial lakes.

steps.action: Choose coring sites from a preceding seismic reflection survey to cover all depocenters, and plan winter coring with an adapted Kullenberg piston corer and gravity corer on a vehicle ferry.
steps.quote: We identified coring sites (Figure 3) through a preceding seismic reflection survey to cover all major LArg depocenters and depositional environments

steps.action: Recover 47 cores (108 m), then scan them (magnetic susceptibility, gamma density, optical line-scan, spectrophotometry), log them, and analyse selected intervals by XRF, LD-PSA and smear slides.
steps.quote: We recovered a total of 108 m of core from 47 sites in August–September 2019

steps.action: Count laminae and measure their thickness with the authors' earlier autocorrelation tool CountMYvarves, which runs multiple simultaneous counts to propagate uncertainty.
steps.quote: sliding-window autocorrelation of digital core scans (CountMYvarves, see a full description in Van Wyk de Vries et al., 2021)

steps.action: Establish that rhythmic light and dark laminae dominate the sediment throughout the basin, thousands of couplets in the main basin and hundreds in the brazos.
steps.quote: Lago Argentino's sediment is dominated by alternating light and dark laminae

steps.action: Decompose the LD-PSA grain-size distributions with an iterative Gaussian mixture model (R2 > 0.95, at most 4 peaks) into fine (~0.5 µm) and coarse (1.8–3.4 µm) endmembers.
steps.quote: Gaussian mixture model separation shows that 80.5% of samples are composed of two endmembers.

steps.action: Check the LD-PSA histograms against the petrographic smear-slide grain sizes.
steps.quote: LD-PSA-derived grain-size histograms are consistent with petrographic observations

steps.action: Fit an exponential decay of 50-year-mean lamina thickness against distance from the Upsala and Perito Moreno fronts (R2 0.37 and 0.40).
steps.quote: Sedimentation rate away from glacier front averaged over the past 50 years shows a moderate fit to an exponential decay

steps.action: Report that XRF shows the eastern margin is compositionally distinct (higher Ca/K, Ti/K), and that dark laminae have higher Ca/K than light laminae.
steps.quote: Coupled sub-mm resolution XRF results reveal that the sediment composition also varies between light and dark lamina.

steps.action: Measure 137Cs profiles by gamma spectrometry in three cores (11A, 20A/20B merged, 27A) and locate the activity peaks.
steps.quote: All three cores analyzed exhibit above-background 137Cs activity

steps.action: Run blanks of the sample containers and duplicate analyses to check the gamma detector for contamination and to estimate precision (±5%); reported in Methods.
steps.quote: Blank runs of u-channels and plastic boxes used to hold the sediment showed no measurable 137Cs activity.

steps.action: Map relative suspended sediment concentration in 77 Sentinel-2 images by season, and identify internal waves in 284 Sentinel-1 radargrams.
steps.quote: Lake surface rSSCs are generally the highest during winter months

steps.action: Ask whether the light and dark laminae are annual (varves).
steps.quote: We first test whether the alternating light and dark lamina are varves.

steps.action: List rival causes of the cyclic lamination: the seasonal cycle, tides, orbital cycles, turbidity currents, an 85-min seiche, and ENSO/SAM multiannual cycles.
steps.quote: A variety of processes may give rise to cyclically laminated sediment, including the [...]

steps.action: Derive the annual-lamina prediction: 44–56 couplets (49–56 for 27A) above the 1963–1965 137Cs horizon, allowing for disrupted top laminae.
steps.quote: Cores were collected in 2019, meaning that 54–56 annual layers should have been deposited since 1963–1965.

steps.action: Compare the depth of the 137Cs horizon with the lamina-count depth in all three cores; they agree within uncertainty (Table 1).
steps.quote: The depth of the 1963–1965 137Cs horizon is within uncertainty of the lamina-count derived depth

steps.action: Reject multiannual climatic cycles and seiches as causes, on lamina number, regularity and thickness.
steps.quote: too thick to result from 1.5 hr period seiches

steps.action: Conclude that the laminae are varves, giving an annual-resolution sedimentation record.
steps.quote: we conclude that the laminations in LArg are annual—they are varves.

steps.action: Assign seasons to the layers: dark, coarse summer layers and light, fine, K-rich winter layers, the reverse of the DeGeer norm.
steps.quote: summer layers in LArg are darker than winter layers

steps.action: Ask which mechanisms produce the seasonal sediment changes, through a conceptual varve-formation model.
steps.quote: We next build a conceptual varve-formation model for LArg and explore the mechanisms that give rise to these seasonal sediment changes.

steps.action: Propose at least two distinct processes: fluvial in the eastern lake, glacial elsewhere.
steps.quote: at least two distinct processes generate varves in LArg

steps.action: Match eastern-margin composition, grain size and the summer-high rSSC plume to the seasonal discharge of Río La Leona.
steps.quote: The results show that the majority of sediment in this eastern margin of LArg is derived from Río La Leona.

steps.action: Set two rival or combined glacial mechanisms: a seasonal cycle in glacial sediment delivery and a seasonal cycle in lake mixing.
steps.quote: a seasonal cycle in glacial sediment delivery and a seasonal cycle in the degree of lake mixing

steps.action: Compute Stokes settling velocities and settling times bracketed by plug-flow and stirred-reactor endmembers (Appendix A), showing that a seasonal influx cycle fractionates coarse from fine grains.
steps.quote: Stokes' Law can therefore be used to compute settling velocities

steps.action: Find that the delivery-only mechanism predicts summer-high rSSC, while winter-high rSSC and weak ice-velocity seasonality are observed.
steps.quote: This is inconsistent with a seasonal cycle in sediment influx alone

steps.action: Compute Richardson numbers for plausible density contrasts and winds and place LArg in Fischer et al. (1979) regimes, with higher summer Ri (Figure 10).
steps.quote: LArg is likely in the “Partially stratified” regime the majority of the time

steps.action: Compare the predicted summer stratification with the internal-wave frequency from Sentinel-1; they are consistent.
steps.quote: This is consistent with more frequent observations of internal waves in the summer than in the winter

steps.action: Estimate the eddy diffusivity at which mixing time equals settling time for 2–4 µm grains (K = 1.8–7.2 × 10^-4 m2/s).
steps.quote: we calculate the eddy diffusivity for which the mixing timescale is equal to the settling timescale

steps.action: Keep a combination of seasonal sediment delivery and seasonal lake mixing as the glacial varve mechanism across most of the lake.
steps.quote: We therefore consider that varves likely result from a combination of the two processes across most of LArg.

steps.action: Set the LArg processes against studies of smaller proglacial lakes and ice-proximal marine settings, and summarize where their relative importance differs.
steps.quote: many processes occurring in LArg are comparable to those in smaller lakes, but that the relative importance of these processes may differ

tree.answer: Rhythmic light/dark laminae throughout a large ice-contact lake
Laminae, grain size and composition are observed directly; lake mixing is only inferred (rSSC, internal waves, Ri)
Test whether the laminae are annual and explain how they form
Seasonal, tidal, orbital, turbidite, seiche and ENSO/SAM cycles; then delivery versus mixing mechanisms
Annual laminae predict 44–56 couplets above the 137Cs horizon; delivery-only predicts summer-high rSSC
Conditions found: natural lake sediment cored in 2019, with the bomb-137Cs horizon as a marker

tree.question: 6b
tree.answer: Nature repeats across 47 cores and 3 dated cores; thickness decays with distance from glacier fronts
Varve claim agrees in all three dated cores; mechanism claim rests on indirect consistency only
Laminae are varves; formed by a combination of delivery and mixing cycles, plus fluvial input in the east
No review record supplied; the acknowledgments mention one named and two anonymous referees

end.claim: The light/dark laminae of Lago Argentino are annual varves (dark coarse summer layers, light fine winter layers), confirmed by 137Cs horizons that agree with lamina counts in three cores.

decisive_move.sentence: Comparing the 1963–1965 137Cs horizon with the lamina-count depth in three cores is what turns rhythmic laminae into dated varves; every later inference uses that annual interpretation.

gates.evidence: Coring sites were chosen to cover depocenters (p. 4), not by a hypothesis. The detailed analyses were designed after the initial logging showed lamination (p. 4). The 137Cs dating was used 'to further test the hypothesis that the light and dark sediment laminae are seasonal' (p. 12). That test could have failed: lamina-count depths could have disagreed with the 137Cs horizon (Table 1). Nothing is reported as fixed before the data were seen.

imports.item: Gaussian mixture model (McLachlan & Peel 2004) for decomposing grain-size distributions
Plug-flow and stirred-reactor endmember models of settling
Richardson number and stratification regimes (Fischer et al. 1979)

limits: Sub-claims at other statuses: the varve-formation mechanisms (combined seasonal delivery and mixing, plus fluvial input in the east) are best_explanation (p. 17, 19); the exponential decay of sedimentation rate with distance from glacier fronts is regularity_in_range, with moderate fit, R2 ~0.4 (p. 7, 17). Seasonal lake mixing is not measured. The authors say they lack 'any direct data on LArg's seasonal changes in lake mixing timescale' (p. 17). The Ri inputs are 'likely' values, not measurements. The rSSC values are uncalibrated (p. 6). XRF counts are uncalibrated (p. 4). Only three cores were 137Cs-dated, and the authors chose the depth of the 137Cs horizon (between the peak and background), which gives wide ranges. The supplement (Figure S1, Table S1) was not supplied. No review file was supplied, so the effect of review is unknown; the acknowledgments mention one named and two anonymous referees. The order of the analyses beyond what the text states (e.g., whether the 137Cs test was planned before lamina counting) is inference.

disagreements.target: DeGeer (1912) varve norm of light summer and dark winter layers
disagreements.support: Grain-size and Ca/K data show that LArg's dark laminae are the coarse summer layers, coloured by dark minerals such as pyroxene, and the light laminae are the K-rich winter clays.
disagreements.quote: Unlike the original light summer layer and dark winter layer varve norm (DeGeer, 1912), summer layers in LArg are darker than winter layers.

disagreements.target: Prior proglacial-lake process studies (Rubensdotter & Rosqvist 2009; Schiefer & Gilbert 2008; Richards et al. 2012; Larsen et al. 2011; [...]
disagreements.support: The authors argue that these studies sampled small alpine lakes, and that in a lake two to three orders of magnitude larger the same processes have different relative importance.
disagreements.quote: Prior studies are, however, strongly biased toward small alpine glacier lakes two to three orders of magnitude smaller than LArg.

alternatives_considered.reason: Manual counting is time consuming, subjective, and hard to reproduce; the automated counts propagate uncertainty

alternatives_considered.chosen: Mean couplet thickness as the depth-average of all lamina thicknesses
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Total lamina count divided by core length
alternatives_considered.reason: Not sensitive to disrupted or missing sediment, such as at core-section breaks

alternatives_considered.chosen: LD-PSA run directly on sediment with no preprocessing
XRF analysed as counts and count ratios
Satellite rSSC treated as a relative measure
alternatives_considered.reason: Limited in-situ SSC measurements for calibration

alternatives_considered.chosen: Coring in winter from a local vehicle ferry
alternatives_considered.reason: Wind speeds are lowest in winter

alternatives_considered.chosen: Both plug-flow and stirred-reactor endmembers, to bracket settling times
alternatives_considered.reason: No direct measurements of water-column turbulence

alternatives_considered.alternatives: Schmidt stability, Lake Number, Wedderburn Number
Tides, orbital cycles, turbidity currents, 85-min seiche, ENSO/SAM multiannual cycles
alternatives_considered.reason: Laminae too numerous and regular for multiannual cycles, too thick for seiches; 137Cs agreement

alternatives_considered.chosen: Combination of a seasonal sediment-delivery cycle and a seasonal lake-mixing cycle
alternatives_considered.alternatives: Sediment-delivery cycle alone; lake-mixing cycle alone
alternatives_considered.reason: Delivery-only is inconsistent with winter-high rSSC; glacier-flow seasonality suggests some delivery cycle; remote sensing and climatology support mixing
